issues.explanation: The trigger set is not clinically coherent with the stated trauma type of witnessed other trauma or with the rest of the profile. 'People cycling' and 'my ex' imply very different personal meanings, and neither has an evident connection to the reported threat items (general unsafety, sleep vigilance, hypervigilance). With only a weak Triggers → Threat link active, the triggers should still plausibly cue the threat state; these two triggers appear idiosyncratic in unrelated directions and are hard to reconcile as part of the same trauma-linked pattern.

vignette:
Karim is a 29-year-old single man of Lebanese descent who works as a train conductor on a commuter line running through the northeastern corridor. He first presented to the clinic six weeks after witnessing a traumatic incident on the job - an event that, by his own account, he had been trying not to think about ever since, with diminishing success.

The incident occurred on a cold morning in late November. Karim was working the early shift when the train struck a pedestrian who had crossed onto the tracks at an unsignalled crossing. He was not driving - that fell to the engineer - but Karim was the first crew member to reach the scene after the train stopped. What he encountered was not something he had been prepared for: a man lying on the gravel embankment, badly injured, with visible wounds that Karim could not look away from fast enough. He remembers the cold most of all - the sharp, biting air against his face and hands as he crouched beside the man and radioed for emergency services. The temperature that morning was in the low thirties, and that particular quality of cold has become inseparable, in his nervous system, from everything that followed.

In the weeks after the incident, Karim found that certain sensory details had taken on a life of their own. Walking to his car on a cold morning, feeling that same bite of winter air against his skin, was enough to pull him back. The cold against his hands - a sensation that had once been unremarkable, even invigorating - now arrived as a signal of something wrong, something dangerous. The sight of blood, even incidentally encountered - a minor cut on a colleague's hand, a news photograph - produced the same lurch. Visible injuries on others, however minor, registered with a force entirely disproportionate to their actual severity. When these triggers arrived, Karim became certain that he was in danger. He had come to believe, with a conviction he could not reason his way out of, that the world around him was fundamentally unsafe - and that the feeling of threat these sensory cues produced was not a memory but a warning. Even when his supervisor told him the incident had been fully reviewed and he had done everything right, even when his mother reminded him he was home and safe, the reassurance passed through him without landing. He was certain that safety was something other people felt, not something available to him.

This sense of unresolvable threat had reorganised his daily life. At night, Karim found it nearly impossible to fall asleep without first checking the locks, the windows, the layout of the room - a ritual that made intellectual sense to him even as he recognised it was excessive. He lay awake scanning for sounds, his body refusing the logic of the quiet apartment. The hypervigilance that had begun on the job had migrated into every environment. On the train, he found himself watching passengers with an attention that exhausted him - tracking movement, monitoring exits, noting who was standing too close to the doors. What had once been a job he took quiet pride in had become a daily ordeal of sustained alertness, and several colleagues had remarked that he seemed different, distant, strung tight. He had not explained why.

The cold weather had become the most immediate practical problem. Winter was deepening, and Karim could not step outside without bracing himself against his own skin. He had begun wearing heavier gloves than the weather required, layering clothing in a way that his coworkers found puzzling, doing what he could to insulate himself from the temperature that kept pulling him back to the embankment and to the man lying there. It helped only partially, and the effort of managing it was constant.

What finally brought Karim to seek help was a morning last week when he stood on the platform before his shift, felt the cold, and found he simply could not board the train. He stood there for several minutes before a colleague came to find him. He has not told anyone what happened. What he is most afraid of is that this will not get better - that the world will stay this dangerous, this unreadable, forever.
